p.rmdir()

strengths: The reciprocal parameterization provides an interpretable empirical description of loss across token positions. The reported R² exceeds 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints, supporting this descriptive finding within the tested settings.

The experiments track two model sizes over 400B training tokens, with checkpoints every 1B tokens. Forecasts from several training prefixes outperform the three reported baselines on both evaluation datasets, providing promising evidence for trajectory prediction.
The position-weighting experiments extend the analysis beyond curve fitting, evaluating three interventions across eight downstream benchmarks and three prompting settings.
weaknesses: Forecast evaluation is insufficiently separated from discovery of the law. Section 3.3 chooses the separation point for best fit on the observed trajectories, which also inform the functional forms. Forecasting prefixes of those same trajectories can therefore give optimistic results even when coefficients use only early checkpoints. The functional forms and separation-point rule should be fixed before evaluation on independent training runs.

The baselines do not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor explicitly incorporates the cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the baselines use simple global curves. Once a0 and a1 are frozen, Equation 10 reduces to a2(N) plus a constant. A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same piecewise logarithmic/cosine structure is essential to establish whether the positional decomposition improves forecasting. The exact power-law baseline is also unspecified and confusingly labeled 'Exponential.'

The conclusion that uniform learning makes position weighting unnecessary exceeds the evidence. Equal changes in position-averaged loss do not establish that alternative weighting cannot improve optimization. Table 2 tests only three fixed suppression heuristics introduced after 100B tokens, without uncertainty estimates or repeated runs; some variants slightly improve the smaller model's average. These results support only the narrower conclusion that the tested interventions provide no clear, consistent advantage.

The scope does not establish a general temporal law: experiments use two nearby model sizes, one training corpus, 1024-token evaluation sequences, and one 400B-token cosine schedule. In particular, the assumed scaling of the separation point with training duration is untested. PG-19 also comes from the Gutenberg domain represented in the Pile, so the OOD evaluation offers limited evidence of generalization to unfamiliar domains.

Reproducibility has material gaps. The appendix promised to contain fitted parameters is absent from the supplied manuscript, and nonlinear-fitting procedures, initialization/constraints, and training batch size are unspecified. Batch size is needed to convert the 2,000 warmup steps into the token count used in Equation 13. Moreover, the stated two-fifths separation point implies 160B tokens, whereas Section 4.1 states 120B. These ambiguities, together with the forecast-validation concerns, prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The novelty framing overstates the absence of prior temporal analysis. Kaplan et al. already investigate learning curves and dependence on training steps. The contribution should be positioned around the empirical positional decomposition and schedule-dependent forecasting construction, with more precise comparisons to existing learning-curve models.
